topic: What if Ancient Rome discovered electricity?
title: WHAT IF ANCIENT ROME
FOUND ELECTRICITY?

power.rule: one spark, and the city answers
power.look: amber electric arcs, a volt dial at 0.7 V and a SPARK chip

script.text: Rome, forty BC. A copper coin. A jar of vinegar. A spark.
A slave's kitchen. The wick dies. Spark. The lamp catches.

script.beat: 1 cold open, demo 3: a cold bath
script.text: A cold bath. Spark. Steam rolls off the water.
A senator's ring. Spark. Every lamp in his villa bows to it.

script.beat: 1 to 2: the rule and the premise
script.text: A spark that jumps. A spark that stays. What if Ancient Rome discovered electricity?
No oil. No smoke. The forum burns bright all night. Hot baths at midnight. Cold wine in summer. The Emperor wants more.
He orders a jar in every house. A wire on every street.

script.beat: 4 the turn: the cost, one real fact
script.text: One catch. A copper jar makes a fiftieth of a watt. About enough to tingle your tongue. To heat one small bath, you need six hundred thousand jars. Rome has nine hundred baths. That's half a billion jars. That's real.
So the Emperor taxes every copper roof in the empire. Temples. Statues. The coins in your hand.

script.beat: 6 a moral choice with family at stake
script.text: Your sister's lamp is next. The legion is at the door. Give them the spark. Or the city goes dark.
Rome doesn't fall to barbarians. It falls to a fuse. Part one.

science.claim: A copper-iron jar in vinegar makes about 0.7 volts and roughly a fiftieth of a watt.
science.working: Standard reduction potentials: Cu2+/Cu +0.34 V, Fe2+/Fe -0.44 V, so the open-circuit cell is 0.78 V; under load about 0.7 V. A large jar with 20 x 20 cm plates and 5% acetic acid has an internal resistance of roughly 5 to 10 ohms: about 0.7 / 10 = 0.07 A short-circuit, and at matched load 0.035 A at 0.35 V, or 0.012 W. With fresh acid and a larger cathode area the matched-load power is about 0.02 W, a fiftieth of a watt. The script says a fiftieth, and the schematic shows 0.7 V.
science.source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, standard electrode potentials; Faraday's law of electrolysis

science.claim: Heating one small Roman bath pool of 10 cubic metres by 25 degrees Celsius takes about 290 kWh, or 600,000 jars working for a day.
science.working: Q = m c dT = 10,000 kg x 4,186 J/(kg K) x 25 K = 1.046e9 J = 290.6 kWh. Spread over 24 hours, that is 1.046e9 / 86,400 = 12.1 kW. At 0.02 W per jar, 12,100 / 0.02 = 605,000 jars. The script rounds to six hundred thousand; the schematic states 605,000.
science.source: Specific heat capacity of water, 4,186 J/(kg K); thermodynamic energy balance

science.claim: Rome's 900 baths would need about half a billion jars.
science.working: The Regionary Catalogues of fourth-century Rome list 856 balnea and 11 thermae, about 867 public baths; the script rounds to nine hundred. 900 x 605,000 = 544,500,000 jars. The schematic counts to 544,500,000 and the script says half a billion.
science.source: Regionary Catalogues of Rome (Curiosum and Notitia), fourth century AD; calculation above
